spin-off from https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2701#issuecomment-2727590885

Current 12.1.5

| # | Description | Level | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **12.1.5** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 12.2.1] Verify that when the application accepts a file, either on its own or within an archive such as a zip file, it checks if the file extension matches an expected file extension and validates that the contents correspond to the type represented by the extension. This includes, but is not limited to, checking the initial 'magic bytes', performing image re-writing, and using specialized libraries for file content validation. | 2 | 434 |


Current 11.3.1
> V11.3.1 Verify that input is validated to **enforce business or functional expectations for that input**. This should either use positive validation against an allowed list of values, patterns or ranges or alternatively be based on comparing to an expected structure or logical limit, according to pre-defined rules. For L1 this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. **For L2 and up, this should apply to all input**.

To be fully aligned with 11.3.1, maybe we need to write some extra piece into 12.1.5 to say, that for files used for "enforce business or functional expectations" must be validated from L1, in general from L2?

comments.body: Do you have an example of a file being used to "enforce business or functional expectations for that input"?

must have - if a file is uploaded as required information to make some business logical decision (e.g. in backoffice), then it must beet the expected structure

nice to have - if a file is uploaded to the application as whetever content or application provides functionality to the end-user to upload and store files, then it is not part of business decision process

I can think of several examples usually reserved for admins.

1) A CSV upload to a IdP with a list of new users
2) A CSV upload of new products to a eCommerce system

The columns in these examples must be perfectly aligned to fit business and functional expectations.

3) Image uploads for a user profile or product image upload

Your business rules may require that profile pictures or product images must be square and fit within certain size limits.

Jim, I think your examples go a bit further from the requirement scope - the requirement asks to validate that the uploaded file is the expected type and format, your examples describe the next step - if the type was expected, it must now be valid for "business logic" rules and actual content expectations.

I hear you Elar. In general, I am in favor of your perspective here and was trying to give examples to answer the questions "... examples of a file being used to "enforce business or functional expectations for that input..."

Some files, like a general file upload system, have no business logic needs. Like a Dropbox or similar.

But some of the more administrative file upload mechanism I have seen need to conform to a significant set of structural, type, ordering and other rules before they will be accepted, like a list of new users.

I'm struggling to give more examples, but am I close to what you were describing?

> I'm struggling to give more examples, but am I close to what you were describing?

yes
Ok so I am comfortable for this to be a split requirement then
I prefer someone else (than me) doing the wordsmithing part here.

So what do we think about  #2748:
